walkthroughs.body_html:
Introduction to Religions (Two from the SL list) — a core area of Religious Studies.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Introduction to Religions (Two from the SL list) brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

mcqs.q: What do orthodox Christians believe about the nature of Jesus?
options: Jesus was a human who became God after his resurrection.
Orthodox Judaism is a different religion from Reform Judaism.
Jesus was half God and half human.
He is fully God and fully human at the same time (the incarnation) — both natures united in one person, as defined at the Council of Chalcedon.

mcqs.q: How does Reform Judaism differ from Orthodox Judaism?
options: Orthodox Judaism is a different religion from Reform Judaism.
Reform Jews don't believe in God and Orthodox Jews do.
Jesus was a human who became God after his resurrection.

Reform Judaism treats Jewish law (halakhah) as evolving and not strictly binding, embraces modernity, and grants gender equality; Orthodox Judaism holds halakhah as divinely given and binding in detail, with traditional practice maintained.

mcqs.q: Is the Buddha a god in Buddhism?
options: No — the Buddha (Siddhartha Gautama) is regarded as an enlightened human teacher who discovered the path to liberation. Theravada Buddhism is generally non-theistic; some Mahayana traditions develop more elaborate cosmologies.
The Buddha created the universe.
Buddhists worship the Buddha as their god.
Orthodox Judaism is a different religion from Reform Judaism.
